leads.candidate: The 1835 Ginkgo near the Joy Street steps, Boston Common
leads.why_a_lead: Per Friends of the Public Garden, the first ginkgo in Boston's parks was transplanted to the Common near the Joy Street steps in 1835, already 40 feet tall at the time, moved from the estate of Mrs. Gardiner Greene (daughter of John Singleton Copley). That would make it a genuinely remarkable, historically documented tree, with a real minimum age (already 40ft when moved in 1835 implies decades of growth before that, likely pushing true age past 200 years). Checked a third time this pass (2026-09-27 deepen): re-fetched the same FoPG ginkgo article in full and ran a fresh web search for 'Joy Street ginkgo Boston Common 1835'; nothing beyond the same single FoPG page turned up anywhere. Still no confirmation this specific 1835 individual is still standing (as opposed to having been one of the Common's ginkgos that has since been replaced), which of the Common's 13 ginkgos it is, or a mappable location beyond 'near the Joy Street steps'. Needs a dedicated look (Friends of the Public Garden tree inventory/map, an arborist record, or an in-person/photo check against the Joy Street steps) to confirm it survives and pin it.

leads.candidate: The last true American Elm on the Common, Railroad Mall
leads.why_a_lead: Friends of the Public Garden identifies this as 'the last true, non-hybridized, American Elm on the Common', located on Railroad Mall just west of the Visitor Information Center. Historically significant (Massachusetts state tree, once-common species nearly wiped out by Dutch Elm Disease, which reached New England in the 1930s-40s, so a genuine survivor is at minimum mature by then). Read the full FoPG 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' article again this pass (2026-09-27 deepen): still a general educational piece about the elm collection across all three parks, not an individual specimen profile, and gives no planting date or age for this tree specifically, only its location and rarity. A fresh targeted web search for a second source (news coverage, Boston Parks Dept, a specific age) again found nothing beyond the same FoPG page. Still single-sourced on age and on existence as a distinct specimen; stays a lead rather than shipping with a guessed age.

leads.candidate: American Elm pair, Public Garden, east of the Marvin Goody Flagpole along Charles St.
leads.why_a_lead: Described by Friends of the Public Garden as large specimens, in the same general 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' article as the Railroad Mall elm above. Being a pair raises the collectible-point question too (would need one obvious place to stand, which a flagpole-adjacent pair plausibly offers, but unverified).

leads.candidate: Rock Elm near the Tool Shed, Public Garden
leads.why_a_lead: Called out by Friends of the Public Garden as 'the lone specimen in the three parks' (Common, Public Garden, Commonwealth Ave Mall), which makes it a genuinely singular, collectible point in principle, and the species itself is notably long-lived (up to ~300 years per general references). Same FoPG 'Meet the Trees: The Elms' source as above, still no age given for this individual after a repeat check this pass. The Arnold Arboretum's own Arnoldia piece on the species ('Ulmus thomasii: The Hard Elm That's Hard to Find', 2016) discusses the species generally and the Arboretum's own specimens, not the Public Garden tree, so it doesn't corroborate this individual. Stays a lead.

leads.candidate: Mount Auburn Cemetery champion trees (28 state champions, 11 New England champions)
leads.why_a_lead: Mount Auburn (Cambridge/Watertown line) is an accredited Level III Arboretum with over 5,300 trees inventoried (1997) including 28 Massachusetts state champions and 11 New England champions, per the cemetery's own 'Champion Trees of Mount Auburn' program. Transit: subway plus the 71 bus from downtown Boston runs about 29 minutes per Rome2rio, or Red Line to Harvard Square then the 71/73 bus roughly 16 minutes, or a 15-20 minute walk from Harvard Square along Brattle St into Mount Auburn St; sits right on the ~30 minute day-trip boundary in the optimistic case and over it once real transfer waits are counted, so label honestly as 'about 30-40 minutes from downtown Boston via Harvard Square' rather than claiming it clears the bar cleanly. This pass (2026-09-27 deepen) found a genuine STATE register that could settle this cleanly: the Massachusetts DCR/Bureau of Forest Fire Control and Forestry 'Legacy Tree Program' (a real, government-run big/champion tree register, per mass.gov) and its 'Massachusetts Legacy Trees' ArcGIS StoryMap (storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/8a672570e4d14887b44152bf61ae92e0). Could not read either one's actual tree-by-tree content this pass: the StoryMap is JS-rendered and returned no substantive content to a fetch, and mountauburn.pastperfectonline.com (the cemetery's own Tree Map/PastPerfect database, tried again this pass) still 403s to automated fetches (candidate for the fetch-blocklist). This is the single most promising unresolved thread for a future pass: a rendering fetch of the StoryMap, or a browser-session look at PastPerfect, would very likely turn up a specific, named, individually locatable Massachusetts state champion at Mount Auburn. Checked the one specific named tree already known here, the Prince of Wales Beech (see below): historically the most famous individual specimen, but it is a 2008-planted graft, not the 1860 original, so it fails 'genuinely old' outright. Per the brief: never pin 'the cemetery' as a tree; this stays a lead until a specific living, aged, individually locatable specimen turns up.

leads.candidate: The Prince of Wales Beech, Mount Auburn Cemetery
leads.why_a_lead: Genuinely remarkable story: planted by the 19-year-old Prince of Wales (future Edward VII) in person on 19 October 1860, a well-documented royal-visit tree with contemporary newspaper coverage. But the original tree developed Beech Tree Decline, was sonically imaged in 2007 (over 50% of trunk wood unsound) and was removed in March 2008 at more than 150 years old. What stands today, planted in a ceremony on 3 May 2008, is a single surviving scion grafted from 1993 cuttings of the original, roughly 18 years old now, genetically identical but not the tree the Prince touched. Under the project's living-succession rule this could ship as an entry describing the living graft honestly (comparable to the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent), but a barely-18-year-old sapling is a stretch for 'ancient trees' and reads better as a story footnote than a collectible point; leaving it as a lead rather than forcing it in. Also unresolved: Mount Auburn's day-trip transit status (see the champion-trees entry above).

leads.candidate: Tree Boston 'Big Old Trees Program' entries (Roxbury Willow at Fort Hill, Dorchester Ginkgo at 31 Tonawanda St, Mattapan Swamp White Oak, East Boston Willow, Hyde Park Pin Oak at Fairview Cemetery)
leads.species: various (Salix alba, Ginkgo biloba, Quercus bicolor, Quercus palustris)
leads.why_a_lead: treeboston.org runs a crowd-nominated 'Big Old Trees' registry with addresses and trunk diameter (DBH) for each: Roxbury Willow (20 Fort Ave, DBH 52in, height 42ft), Dorchester Ginkgo (31 Tonawanda St, DBH 41.5in, height 93.7ft), Mattapan Swamp White Oak (201-211 River St, DBH 42in), East Boston Willow (East Boston Memorial Ballpark, DBH 46in), Hyde Park Pin Oak (45 Fairview Ave, Fairview Cemetery, DBH 44in). None carry an age estimate anywhere on the page, only DBH/height, and the registry is explicitly self-reported/nomination-based rather than professionally dated. Estimating age from DBH alone without a species-specific growth-rate source would be a guess dressed as a fact, so still not verifiable on age. They are also scattered across outer Boston neighbourhoods rather than forming a walkable cluster. Each would need an actual age source (arborist record, core sample, planting record) and a second confirming source before it could verify.

leads.candidate: Mount Auburn Cemetery and Forest Hills Cemetery, specific named champion/specimen trees
leads.why_a_lead: Checked again this pass with fresh searches for a single named, individually locatable specimen at either cemetery. Mount Auburn: the 'Champion Trees of Mount Auburn' event page still names no individual tree, species or location; see the dedicated Mount Auburn lead above for the Massachusetts Legacy Tree Program / StoryMap thread that is the likely way to close this. Forest Hills Cemetery (in Jamaica Plain, actually within Boston city limits, so it would clear the day-trip question that Mount Auburn does not): general sources describe 'an unusual collection of large specimen trees, some introduced by the Arnold Arboretum' including cherry, sugar and Japanese maple, umbrella pine and weeping hemlock, but nothing names a single tree with location or age. Both stay leads until a dedicated fetch of the actual tree-map/inventory tools turns up one specific, pinnable specimen.

leads.candidate: The Washington Elm successor sapling, Cambridge Common
leads.why_a_lead: The original Washington Elm (Garden St / Mason St junction, where Washington supposedly took command of the Continental Army in 1775) died and was removed in 1923; a bronze marker set flush in the pavement is all that is confirmed to remain there (per History Cambridge's dedicated 'Washington Elm Debate Rages On' article). A general web search snippet separately claimed 'a sapling of the iconic elm was planted in the Common by Vice President Charles Dawes on April 19, 1925, and that tree is the one that stands in Cambridge Common today', but the History Cambridge article itself, which covers the same 1925 sesquicentennial commemoration in detail, describes only a parade and the bronze plaque, concluding 'now nothing remains'. Genuinely contradictory between a search-engine summary and the dedicated primary source; not resolved this pass either. If a Dawes sapling was in fact planted in 1925 and survives, it would be a ~101-year-old tree and a strong day-trip-boundary-clearing (Cambridge Common is central, no transit issue) candidate under the living-succession precedent. Needs a dedicated look at Cambridge Common's own tree inventory or the Cambridge Historical Commission before shipping either way.

Logged as a fresh clue for whoever next works this lead rather than acted on; not enough to pin or verify this pass either.

leads.candidate: The Waverley Oak(s), Beaver Brook Reservation, Belmont/Waltham line
leads.why_a_lead: New this pass (2026-09-27 deepen), found via the Massachusetts DCR's own 'Legacy Tree Program' StoryMap (an official state register, fetched via its underlying ArcGIS item data JSON since the rendered page is JS-only), which names it as a Legacy Tree: 'A small portion of the cluster of 22 White Oaks (Quercus alba) have existed for over six centuries... one enormous tree, believed to be a descendant of the original specimens, continues to stand strong within the park today.' Beaver Brook Reservation (66 Mill St, Belmont, on the Belmont/Waltham line) is within the day-trip boundary, reachable by MBTA bus from Harvard or Alewife in well under 30 minutes. HOWEVER this is a genuine alive/dead conflict across sources, not just a thin one, so it is held rather than shipped despite the register-alone allowance: Wikipedia's 'Beaver Brook Reservation' article states flatly 'the last of the ancient trees succumbed to old age in the 1920s' with no mention of a survivor; a 2020 tree-walk blog (everyoneoutdoors.blogspot.com) says the original oaks are 'once found' on the property, i.e. gone, and describes only their unrelated replacements; a Dec 2025 blog (backsideofamerica.blogspot.com), quoting the Waverley Trail's own site, says 'none of those mighty oaks are still standing' but that 'descendants... stand today' with no specific tree named. Against that, a 2015 comment on treenotes.blogspot.com (Jim Luckett) is specific and detailed: 'The one remaining very old oak at the site is at the corner of Wilson and Waverley Oaks Rds, near Trapelo Rd. There is a sign... It's about 4 1/2 feet in diameter which makes it about 250 years old,' which if true would make it one of the ORIGINAL grove (250 years old in 2015 implies planted c.1765, consistent with the 1790s-and-earlier grove), not a mere descendant sapling, and would directly contradict the 'none survive' claims. That comment is now 11 years old and unconfirmed by anything more recent. The Waverley Trail's own site (waverleytrail.org) places an interpretive kiosk 'opposite the intersection of Trapelo and Mill Street, just inside the stone wall,' a DIFFERENT corner from the one the 2015 comment names, adding a location conflict on top of the alive/dead one. Two fetch attempts on Historic New England's own March-2025-indexed photo of 'Waverly Oaks, Belmont' (gusn/386015) both 403'd (candidate for the fetch-blocklist) and could not settle it. Needs a satellite/aerial look at the Trapelo/Mill and Wilson/Waverley Oaks Rd corners, or a more recent ground report, before this ships either way.
